title: The First Undertakings
summary: Original foundational canon linking the First Reckoning, the costs of ancestor law, and the uncanny conditions inherited by the later basin. These entries synthesize the wiki’s source-derived histories; they are not additional random draws.
source_notes: Original synthesis of the world’s foundational institutions.

entries.title: The First Reckoning
entries.inspiration: Original world chronology, developed from the distinction between political titles, actual provisioning, and finite institutional coordination.
entries.body:
The First Reckoning did not count the dead. It counted promises whose speakers had died, a distinction preserved in the oldest inscription beneath Vey’s public landing. Before the Reckoning, each ruling household dated obligations by the reign that authenticated them. When a ruler fell, successors announced a new beginning. The water did not reliably cooperate. Gates resisted opening, fields salted unevenly, and households discovered that changing a seal could not discharge a predecessor’s witnessed commitment.

The immediate crisis concerned a ferry whose grain portion had been pledged twice. One dead keeper had promised a fixed amount to workers repairing its landing; his successor had promised the same stored grain to people sheltering flood survivors. Both agreements were credible. The landing households tried washing the successor’s mark from the boat. That act changed nothing except the appearance of the hull. They eventually divided available grain, negotiated remaining portions with surviving claimants, and repaired a second landing so the ferry could earn the balance.

Readers from six cities adopted a common count of years to prevent future rulers from hiding obligations inside incompatible reign calendars. They did not elect a basin sovereign. Each city retained its courts and rites, and several refused the count for generations. Year zero therefore marks an agreement about records, not creation, universal revelation, or the first appearance of the dead. Traditions describing it as the morning water learned human names are beautiful and historically unproved.

The first lists also recorded uncertainty. A damaged tally was not repaired by inventing a comforting obligation. An unnamed claimant was not assumed to be nobody. These practices influenced the later Faceted Water Council, whose founders expanded coordination but repeatedly mistook it for general authority.

In 1248, the Reckoning still helps people compare accounts across fallen regimes. Its original ferry has vanished; its landing has been rebuilt at least nine times. A small shelf beneath the present kitchen holds an ordinary bowl for obligations still under inquiry. The bowl has no known supernatural effect. Its significance is the pause it creates before an official declares that a change of ruler has solved somebody else’s unfinished life.

entries.title: The Doubly Held
entries.inspiration: Original bodily consequence of incompatible valid claims, connecting material evidence, discrete manifestations, and the limits of control over the dead.
entries.body:
A doubly held person is not possessed by two personalities. Two incompatible undertakings have acquired a valid claim upon the same repeated bodily act: a hand pouring water, a foot entering a landing, a mouth reciting a witnessed portion. Most people carrying such obligations experience nothing extraordinary. In a small number of well-documented cases, the affected act divides. A hand pours while its owner feels it remain clenched; a footprint appears on the opposite side of a basin; a spoken name arrives from behind the speaker before the lips move.

The effect requires the specific water and observance attached to the claims. Away from that place, the person ordinarily regains an undivided movement. This gives flight genuine protective value, although leaving can also mean losing a livelihood, a dependent relative, or the only recognized witness to an inheritance. Courts that describe departure as an easy remedy ignore those costs.

The condition consumes something local. A split pouring can drain a cistern faster than the visible amount explains. Repeated divided steps can leave the neighboring soil crusted with salt. No case has produced a useful second worker or an unlimited supply of motion. Patrons who tried employing afflicted people as doubled labor damaged their own water and injured the people they claimed to be studying.

Relief begins by identifying the actual undertakings. An interpreter who confidently names two angry ancestors without documentary support can make the person dependent on an invented cure. The Unpressed Consent Rule is valuable here: a blank or silent claimant cannot simply be assigned the terms convenient to a court. In some cases, negotiated substitution separates the obligations. In others, an observance is moved with claimant consent or the site is abandoned.

Those restored retain different memories of the divided act. Some regard it as contact with the dead; some remember pressure and fear only. The condition supplies no proof that its sufferers are morally compromised. Their overlapping obligations may result from an adoption, a forged expansion of a genuine claim, or kindness offered during an emergency. Keth’s hospice keeps a room whose water is carried from an unrelated spring, providing temporary ordinary movement while the slower work of inquiry continues.

entries.title: The Mother of the Kept Breath
entries.inspiration: Original myth joining inherited recitation, finite hospitality, and remembrance transmitted through differing versions.
entries.body:
Avel’s oldest account of ancestor law concerns Ilem, a woman waiting beside a flooded landing for children who could not cross. She promised to keep a cup of air beneath an overturned bowl until they arrived. The children were real people in some versions and the names of unborn islands in others. Ilem died before the crossing. When survivors lifted the bowl, a single breath remained beneath it and disturbed the water after every ordinary wind had ceased.

No surviving object authenticates the story. The overturned bowl shown at three island shrines cannot belong to all three versions, and none has a reliable custody chain reaching an uncounted age. Their keepers generally acknowledge this. They preserve the vessels as teaching objects, not as proof that all basin law derives from one woman or one island. Mainland collectors are less cautious and have repeatedly offered money for the most ancient-looking example.

The tradition explains a limit more often than an origin. Ilem keeps one breath for particular children, not endless air for everyone. She does not escape death or appoint her descendants rulers of the sea. Her act remains incomplete until its intended recipients arrive or credible successors agree upon another use. Young listeners sometimes find that ending disappointing. Teachers ask whether a promise becomes less valuable because it cannot repair the whole world.

A darker version says the breath never belonged to Ilem. She borrowed it from something already waiting beneath the landing, and human undertakings are attempts to account for that older loan. Reciters disagree about whether the something was a drowned household, a beast without a mouth, or simply the water’s unclaimed pressure. None of those descriptions has been confirmed.

The tradition continues in ordinary hospitality. Hosts place one empty cup for an expected traveler and remove it after an explicitly stated interval. They avoid promising a universal welcome their stores could not support. Teachers of the progressive coastal lessons use the story without requiring children to believe it. In 1248 its strongest shared teaching is modest: remembrance may keep an act available, but the living must still decide how to complete it without turning one finite kindness into a claim upon everyone who comes later.

entries.title: The Door That Opens for No One
entries.inspiration: Original ruin connecting an oracle’s bounded voice with the drowned chamber’s unresolved antiquity.
entries.body:
The name is misleading. The doorway opens easily, and people who cross it usually return without injury. What it does not do is admit a person to the chamber visible beyond it. A traveler steps through beneath a low stone lintel and emerges beside the cistern approach they left, having completed a short circuit nobody can reconcile with the surrounding masonry. Carrying a measured rope produces an ordinary loop. Sending a dry object through without a person leaves it lying on the apparent chamber floor, inaccessible from the returned path.

There are six inspected accounts and many unreliable ones. The inspected accounts agree about the location and duration but not the room’s contents. One traveler saw a broken bench, another a row of empty supports, another shallow water reflecting a ceiling absent from the exterior survey. No account establishes treasure, a sleeping god, or a universal route into death. Visitors seeking those things have supplied the more spectacular stories.

The doorway stands above the drowned chamber reached by Liwen’s bronze bell. His measurements establish old masonry beneath it without showing that the two spaces share a functioning entrance. Patrons who claim an ancient capital here are relying on resemblance and political hope, not a confirmed plan of the ruin. The Inspection Is Not Title Rule applies with particular force: reaching an extraordinary threshold does not purchase ownership of the people maintaining its approach.

Its only repeatable material cost is water lost from a nearby plaster cistern after a crossing. The amount varies with the visitor’s wet footwear, not rank or declared purpose. Custodians limit trials and require provision for that loss. They forbid leaving people inside deliberately, a prohibition adopted after a frightened apprentice was told that obedience would prove his household’s innocence. The apprentice returned through the ordinary loop, but the attempted coercion remains recorded.

One lintel mark may indicate a household undertaking whose intended claimant is extinct. If that reading is correct, the apparent room might be available only to somebody the living cannot honestly appoint. If it is wrong, generations of legal interpretation have been imposed on an older phenomenon. Custodians preserve both possibilities. They maintain the roof, admit careful inquiry, and refuse the profitable promise that a sufficiently worthy adventurer will be allowed through.

entries.title: The Last Season of an Extinct House
entries.inspiration: Original mechanism for finite release, developed from cultural succession, practical care, and the difference between a title and an executable duty.
entries.body:
An extinct household can retain a valid undertaking without leaving a recognized person able to consent to its revision. The Last Season practice addresses that difficulty through a deliberately narrow substitute. Custodians identify the promised act, the surviving benefit, and the people currently bearing its cost. They appoint a temporary recipient for one season, witnessed by households with conflicting interests. Successful provision does not make the substitute the extinct family’s heir in every other matter.

The oldest documented case concerns a garden pledged to supply fruit for a hospice whose founders died without recognized descendants. Later owners maintained the delivery but could not change a route made dangerous by a collapsed channel. An interpreter demanded continuing obedience until a true heir appeared. Gardeners and patients instead chose one care worker to receive the fruit through a safer landing for a single harvest. Nothing destructive followed, and the hospice’s records show the intended provision continued.

The practice does not prove the dead approve whatever living people decide. Failed substitutions are recorded too. A wealthy claimant once appointed his own servant and diverted a portion into private stores; the affected spring lost usable water until the original amount was restored. The inquiry established a specific failure of provision, not a general right for the claimant to condemn unrelated households.

Some courts reject Last Season because it admits uncertainty about the recipient. Others abuse it by declaring inconvenient houses extinct before checking migrants, unrecognized children, and adopted kin. Vesh’s methods are useful safeguards: absence in one register must not become a convenient conclusion about a whole person’s life. A substitute is accepted only after documented inquiry and must remain answerable to people who might contradict it.

In 1248 the practice gives several doubly held people a possible route to undivided movement. It also supports repairs where an old agreement’s purpose survives but its original form cannot. The season’s ending matters. Custodians must review what happened rather than let temporary authority quietly become inherited jurisdiction. Its hope is neither universal absolution nor endless submission: a specific useful promise may be completed or carried forward in a form the living can actually sustain.

entries.title: Dry Copies and Wet Witnesses
entries.inspiration: Original distinction organizing the Markdown-like in-world archive: records can carry evidence without generating binding consent.
entries.body:
A dry copy can establish what somebody said, where an object traveled, or which portion remains unpaid. It cannot create the undertaking it describes. A clerk may copy a promise perfectly and still lack the speaker’s consent, the actual water contact, or the credible second witness required for the promise to survive death. This distinction makes ordinary archives useful without turning every copied mistake into a supernatural burden.

Water contact alone is equally insufficient. A child splashing beside a game has not agreed to every rule written by a patron elsewhere. A person singing a wordless air cannot endorse a charter whose terms were never stated. The living often try to expand consent through these shortcuts because direct negotiation is slower, less flattering, and capable of producing refusal. The basin’s courts differ in how well they resist that pressure.

The wet witness need not remain alive forever. Evidence can pass through custody, independent accounts, material observance, and testimony about what the witness actually heard. None supplies unlimited certainty. A genuine bowl authenticates its own history only within what surviving evidence establishes; it does not make every prestigious story attached to it true. The Heirs’ Drowned Room is dangerous precisely because a valid object and a missing account can preserve incompatible halves of a claim.

Dispersed catalog houses carry dry references between regions, allowing a local inquiry to find evidence far away. This has widened access and created new risks when a reference exposes a vulnerable household’s location. The Withheld Location Clause permits private inspection through a trusted custodian, preserving accountability without assuming that every useful fact must be shouted in a crowded yard.

The First Reckoning’s achievement was to record obligations beyond the life of a ruling seal. Its continuing danger is the temptation to treat the record as the obligation itself. In 1248, careful readers still begin with three separate questions: what happened, what was agreed, and what can now be performed. An elegant manuscript can assist each inquiry. It cannot answer all three merely by being old, beautifully made, or guarded by an influential house.
